title: Context degradation micro-notes (Mira Silva)
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad to collect observations, half-baked ideas, and small experiments about how models degrade as context length grows and strategies to measure and mitigate it. Not a polished note — intentionally choppy.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Contextual degradation seems to arise from two interacting factors: cache/kv precision loss (numerical + sparsity) and distributional drift of the model's attention over longer sequences.
- Short-term experiments: contrast prefix-preserving caching vs periodic re-encoding; measure answer drift on synthetic stepwise QA.
- Longer-term: build a tiny benchmark that mixes coherent, adversarial, and irrelevant context chunks to quantify resiliency.

Key observations from recent reading (quick bullets):
- Paper A (notes): shows that attention weight spread increases with sequence length; effective receptive field shrinks for important tokens. Hypothesis: attention dilution + KV quantization amplifies.
- Blog post B (practical): engineers reported that re-embedding a compact representation of earlier context regained about ~6-12% of answer fidelity on short tasks — cheap and promising.
- Distillation notes: compressing long context into a short latent (e.g., learned summary tokens) can help but risks removing salient rare facts (edge-case loss).

Ideas to test (ranked):
1) Controlled synthetic chain-of-thought QA drift test
   - Setup: generate 8k-token contexts composed of 4 sections: (1) factual base, (2) distractors, (3) chain-of-thought steps that lead to an answer, (4) final question.
   - Metric: exact-match on final answer, plus an embedding-similarity drift per section.
   - Variables: model size (7B vs 70B), kv-precision (fp16/8-bit/4-bit), cache span (full vs sliding window).

2) Prefix-preserve vs rolling-encode tradeoff
   - Prefix-preserve: keep early key/value entries frozen in KV cache and only update later tokens. Cheaper but may cause mismatch if model expects updates.
   - Rolling-encode: periodically re-encode a compressed prefix (e.g., one dense vector per 512 tokens) and feed as special tokens.
   - Measure latency, tokens saved, and fidelity.

3) Adversarial chunk insertion
   - Insert semantically similar distractor chunks that mimic salient facts but are wrong. Evaluate model's susceptibility as function of chunk position and length.

Simple eval plan (mini-benchmark):
- 300 prompts * 3 difficulty tiers (easy/medium/hard); each prompt has 6 context variants (clean, early-distractor, late-distractor, repeated-facts, paraphrase, compressed-prefix).
- Run across 3 quantization configs and 2 cache policies. Track: EM, token-latency, top-k token probability shift at answer time.
- Visuals: heatmap of EM vs chunk position; per-prompt time series of predicted-answer probability.

Practical mitigation patterns (brainstorm):
- Lightweight re-encoding: every N tokens compute a 128-d summary vector; prepend to KV cache as summary tokens that are never evicted.
- Weighted attention bias: increase attention logits on tokens that were high-salience earlier (need salience heuristic).
- Retrieval-style anchors: store canonical facts in a small on-disk KV store that can be re-injected deterministically when question topics map.
- Conservative fallback: if model confidence drops below threshold, re-run with compressed prefix re-encode.

Micro-experiments I ran (notes):
- Local toy model (7B) with sliding window of 2048 + simple kv-evict reduced EM by ~9% when distractors placed at 1.5k tokens behind.
- Re-encoding every 1024 tokens (one CLS-like token) recovered ~4% EM at cost of +12ms/token.
- Observed that quantizing KV to 8-bit increased drift variance — answers oscillated more across seeds.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is degradation more from attention distribution change or numeric conditioning in KV? Need an ablation that swaps KV but keeps attention (hard).
- How does instruction-following tasks vs retrieval tasks differ in sensitivity? Intuition: retrieval tasks rely more on token-level fidelity; instructions degrade more gracefully.
- Do compression strategies (PCA vs learned MLP) preserve low-frequency facts differently?

Small TODO list (short horizon):
- [ ] Implement synthetic chain-of-thought generator (templated) — due 2024-12-12.
- [ ] Add metric hooks: per-token answer-prob trace + embedding drift export.
- [ ] Run 7B baseline experiments on dedicated infra (ask SRE for short slot).
- [ ] Draft a tiny confluence page with experiment plan and a table for runs. Link: confluence:INF-482-context-playbook (placeholder).

Notes to self (quick heuristics):
- When designing distractors, vary lexical overlap independently from semantic similarity.
- Use beam-sampling to capture multimodal output behavior — some degradation may cause model to switch modes rather than slowly shift.
- Track randomness: run each config with 3 seeds and median/iqr.

Potential pitfalls / ethical considerations:
- Synthetic adversarial contexts could be used to craft poisoning attacks; keep dataset internal and redact real user prompts.
- When proposing fallbacks that re-run model, consider cost tradeoffs and rate limits — might harm latency-sensitive customers.

References & quick links (for return visits):
- arXiv placeholder: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12345 (context attention spread study)
- Practical post: https://engineering-blog.example.com/context-compression
- Internal playbook note: confluence:INF-482-context-playbook

Last quick thoughts:
- Focus early on small, interpretable tests (synthetic QA) before scaling to real user logs.
- If re-encoding baseline looks promising, try hybrid: keep compressed prefix + stem KV entries for very high-salience tokens.

End of scratchpad.

(Mira)
